claim: Googlebook ships a built-in Linux development environment: a Debian VM managed by the Terminal app.
platform_scope: Googlebook Android host; built-in Debian Terminal VM
what_it_establishes: Official Google documentation retrieved 2026-10-16 (Terminal preview post published 2026-10-12; Terminal support page) describes the Debian VM as a current shipping Googlebook feature with VM settings, shared folders and port-forwarding workflows. Guest-native Debian packages are the intended execution environment.
what_it_does_not_establish: Guest Debian release, ABI, kernel, package set, mount paths, storage semantics, POSIX fidelity or restart durability; those require the S00.02 guest inventory and FS probes on hardware.

claim: The Terminal VM supports automatic localhost port forwarding to the host browser, with user-visible controls (auto-forward and per-port adds).
platform_scope: Googlebook host browser to built-in Debian VM
what_it_establishes: The Terminal preview post documents automatic localhost port forwarding to the host browser; the support page documents 'Auto-forward all ports' and '+ Add port' controls and the Files app VM view.
what_it_does_not_establish: Ordinary-APK native-socket or WebView reachability, forwarding internals, or behavior with forwarding disabled/removed. Host-browser forwarding is not a universal third-party socket API; Chrome-only success cannot certify an APK route.

claim: Terminal start is user-driven; in AOSP source the Terminal app exposes an exported MainActivity (action android.virtualization.VM_TERMINAL) while VmLauncherService is not exported (stopWithTask=true) and the application defaults to enabled=false.
platform_scope: AOSP Virtualization module (moving main branch, retrieved 2026-10-16); shipping Googlebook package may differ
what_it_establishes: Source-level launch topology of the AOSP Terminal app: the launch activity is exported, the VM launcher service is unexported, and the app is default-disabled. A launch action is not a guest command-execution or VM-control API.
what_it_does_not_establish: The shipping Googlebook Terminal package identity or behavior (GB-DEV-005 records the observed package), any right to bind the unexported service, or a public launch/launch-and-control contract for third parties.

claim: No documented public API was found by which an ordinary third-party APK can control the existing Terminal VM, execute guest commands, acquire its VM lifetime reference, or grant folders to it (bounded negative search finding, 2026-10-16).
what_it_establishes: Targeted official-source searches on 2026-10-16 (third-party VM, folder, USB and Antigravity integration queries) surfaced no such API. Antigravity's 'Start Antigravity Service' text is onboarding copy, not a binder contract. This grounds ADR-0001 decision A4 (user-driven bootstrap baseline).
what_it_does_not_establish: That no such API can ever exist. Any future publication flips this claim, reopens ADR-0001 A4 and the reopen-before-coding list [R01][R02][R03][R04][R05][R07][R08].

claim: Under AOSP's documented virtualization architecture, a VM lives while at least one IVirtualMachine reference is held and shuts down when the last reference is dropped; no documented mechanism hands such a reference to a third-party APK.
platform_scope: AOSP VirtualizationService (generic architecture); Googlebook Terminal ownership not documented for third parties
what_it_establishes: The reference-counted VM lifetime mechanism as documented 2026-10-16 (page updated 2026-10-09). Launching the activity or running a foreground service in another APK does not, by declaration, acquire Terminal's VM reference.
what_it_does_not_establish: Googlebook Terminal's exact service topology, actual VM survival on this device across lock/sleep/task-close/force-stop (LIFE-01..04 scenario scope, outside this ledger's probe vocabulary), or any APK-side keepalive claim.

claim: VM lifetime independent of the Terminal window/app, VM and window separation, and dynamic resource scaling are announced future work in Google's Terminal preview, not available capabilities.
what_it_establishes: The 2026-10-12 preview post lists these as roadmap. Product design must show a Terminal dependency and honest VM-unavailable states instead of promising window-independent VM lifetime.
what_it_does_not_establish: Any current independent-lifetime behavior. Roadmap items must never be marked available in plans, ledgers or UI, and never become a dependency.

claim: Terminal documentation includes an alternative graphics screen control for Linux GUI output.
what_it_establishes: The support page retrieved 2026-10-16 documents a GUI 'alternative graphics screen'; a blanket claim of 'no Linux GUI support at all' would be false.
what_it_does_not_establish: Desktop-integrated X11/wayland forwarding, an app-launcher experience, or a supported integration surface for GBCode. This project's UI does not depend on it (ADR-0001 A5).

claim: Integrated Linux GUI experience with app launcher, GPU/NPU acceleration and related graphics work are roadmap items in the Terminal preview.
what_it_establishes: These are announced future work as of 2026-10-16, supporting the decision to render the IDE UI in Android (WebView-hosted original workbench) rather than await Linux GUI support.
what_it_does_not_establish: Current availability of any listed item; they remain unavailable in all plans and must not gate or excuse any design choice.

claim: Android restricts non-SDK interfaces; the presence of a private or hidden API does not imply application access, stability, or permission to depend on it.
what_it_establishes: Google's documented interface policy backing ADR-0001 decisions A1/A2: GBCode integrates only through public SDK surfaces; hidden APIs, undocumented privileges and undocumented services are banned.
what_it_does_not_establish: An inventory of hidden interfaces that exist on Googlebook. For design purposes, absence from the public SDK is treated as unavailability.

claim: Antigravity on Googlebook demonstrates the dual-grant pattern: users grant the same folder to both the Antigravity app and Terminal apps, and its instructions require keeping the Terminal app open.
what_it_establishes: A first-party precedent that separate per-application folder grants plus an explicit Terminal-open dependency is a workable product shape; the Terminal requirement is evidence of a real lifecycle dependency, not an inconvenience to hide. Antigravity is documented as beta and pre-installed on supported models.
what_it_does_not_establish: A public Antigravity/Terminal SDK, binder or service contract, shared UID, privilege delegation, or that GBCode can control Terminal the way first-party Antigravity appears to. Package presence on a device (GB-DEV-006) is not an integration API.

claim: An ordinary (non-privileged) APK can reach Terminal-forwarded VM ports from native sockets and WebView on the target Googlebook.
platform_scope: Target Googlebook device; native APK network stack and WebView to built-in Debian VM
what_it_establishes: Nothing yet; this is the project's first feasibility gate. Only host-browser forwarding is documented (GB-PLAT-002).
what_it_does_not_establish: No pass exists in either direction. Chrome access, emulator runs or documentation cannot certify this; a fail here blocks the APK architecture (containment: connected-IDE routes). Bidirectional HTTP/WebSocket, IPv4/IPv6, permission states and post-Terminal-close behavior are all open.

claim: Android 17 local-network permission rules are target-SDK-dependent and documented to apply across all networking APIs (target >= 37 uses ACCESS_LOCAL_NETWORK; target < 37 with INTERNET receives a temporary implicit grant; Android 16 restriction is opt-in via NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES).
platform_scope: Android 16/17 networking policy (generic), including the open WebView-renderer question
what_it_establishes: The retrieved rule set as of 2026-10-16: enforcement varies by target SDK, denial can surface as TCP timeout or UDP EPERM, and the restriction is documented for all networking APIs.
what_it_does_not_establish: How the rule classifies the Terminal loopback/VM route on this device, whether the WebView renderer inherits the host app's grant, or the target-36 vs 37 grant/deny/revoke matrix on the actual build. A search snippet claiming WebView permission inheritance was absent from the retrieved page body and must not be cited as DOC.

claim: The actual Android WebView renderer on the target device provides the features the Code-OSS workbench needs (secure context, workers, service workers, WebSocket, clipboard in user gesture, extension-resource origin behavior, IME and keyboard input).
platform_scope: Target Googlebook device; WebView renderer hosting the workbench
what_it_establishes: Nothing yet. Desktop Chrome comparisons are controls only; vendor documentation describes requirements, not this renderer's behavior (WebView provider observed in GB-DEV-004).
what_it_does_not_establish: Any certification. Failures must be preserved as evidence; user-agent tricks and SSL bypasses are not acceptable remedies (a tested origin/gateway remedy may be).

claim: Backend documentation states Code-OSS webviews require service workers and secure contexts to function.
what_it_establishes: code-server's FAQ (retrieved 2026-10-16) lists service-worker and secure-context prerequisites; upstream Webview API documentation requires asWebviewUri resource conversion, localResourceRoots restriction and CSP, and states localResourceRoots alone is not complete protection.
what_it_does_not_establish: That the target WebView satisfies these prerequisites (GB-WEB-001, probe WEB-02), or that code-server's same-origin webview patch is an isolation proof; it is a security-review surface, not a demonstrated safe embedding.

claim: Terminal exposes a shared-folder workflow in which the user explicitly adds directories, and Android documents per-app SAF grants; the product plan therefore requires two independent grants (APK and Terminal) for one directory.
platform_scope: Googlebook host storage; Terminal shared folders plus Android SAF
what_it_establishes: Documented user workflows: Terminal's 'Shared folders' setting, Antigravity's grant-both-apps instruction (GB-PLAT-010), and SAF tree-URI grants with persisted permission state.
what_it_does_not_establish: That two grants yield one same-bytes directory view on this device, the guest mount path, or any POSIX guarantee; that identification is exactly what the FS-01 nonce test must show.

claim: Android storage access returns content URIs from user selection, not filesystem paths; Android 30+ blocks selecting storage roots, the Download directory, and Android/data and Android/obb as specified.
what_it_establishes: The documented grant/URI model constraining how GBCode may address the shared directory; supports the rule that guest mapping is discovered from user-selected candidates, never a hard-coded /mnt/... assumption.
what_it_does_not_establish: The guest-side view of a SAF-selected directory, or that Terminal can mount arbitrary third-party DocumentsProviders with suitable POSIX behavior; a custom provider stays a non-default option pending its own small proof (R52).

claim: A directory granted to both the APK and Terminal maps to the identical guest directory with bidirectional byte fidelity on the target device.
platform_scope: Target Googlebook device; APK SAF grant plus Terminal shared folder into built-in Debian VM
what_it_establishes: Nothing yet. Candidate mapping must be derived from actual mount information (e.g. guest findmnt) and verified by bidirectional nonce files.
what_it_does_not_establish: Any mapping claim. A missing or wrong mapping blocks workspace onboarding rather than being papered over; no silent substitute directory or false success indication is acceptable.

claim: The shared-folder semantics real workloads need (case-only rename, Unicode normalization, executable bits, symlinks, atomic replace, watcher delivery, Git operation fidelity) behave adequately on the target device.
platform_scope: Target Googlebook device; shared-directory semantics as seen by guest Linux tools
what_it_establishes: Nothing yet; FS-02 through FS-07 define the measurement matrix (names and encodings, Git workload, execute bits and native modules, watchers, revoked grants and disk-full, concurrent edits).
what_it_does_not_establish: Any assumption that SAF-backed or fused storage provides desktop-POSIX behavior. Managed-native mode remains a distinct, explicitly chosen fallback, never a silent pass for a failed sharing requirement.

claim: Android documents a public serial API at API level 37: android.hardware.serial.SerialManager, SerialPort and SerialPortResponse, with enumeration, port listeners and asynchronous user-approved exclusive open returning a ParcelFileDescriptor.
what_it_establishes: The documented surface and exception model as retrieved 2026-10-16 (SecurityException on rejected user request, IllegalStateException for missing port, IOException on open failure; fd closed by the client). It is distinct from older hidden serial classes.
what_it_does_not_establish: That any Googlebook ships the service or exposes attached ports, driver binding, exclusivity in practice, or termios/control-line behavior; documented availability is not device-driver certification. Serial success cannot certify raw USB/JTAG or replace USB/IP.

claim: The API-37 serial service is present and functional on the target Googlebook (ports visible, open authorized, fd usable).
what_it_establishes: Nothing yet; this is optional fallback support only and is explicitly not a prerequisite for the raw-USB exporter or the default USB/IP profile.
what_it_does_not_establish: Driver binding, exclusive-lease behavior, sustained transfer integrity, or detach semantics on the device (SER-01 first; SER-03/04/08 follow only if the service exists).

claim: esptool's current documentation excludes native USB-OTG and USB-Serial-JTAG ports from remote rfc2217:// and socket:// usage because their local USB VID/PID metadata is unavailable to the remote transport.
platform_scope: esptool remote serial ports (vendor documentation); ESP32-S3 native controllers
what_it_establishes: A documented tool-level boundary retrieved 2026-10-16: RFC2217/socket bridging is not a valid fallback path for the ESP32-S3 native Serial/JTAG; any RFC2217 work must be separately certified against actual USB-UART bridges.
what_it_does_not_establish: Behavior of other tools, or that RFC2217 to a real UART bridge fails (that is SER-05 scope, including baud/control-line negotiation). pySerial notes neither URL handler authenticates or encrypts.

claim: Android's USB host APIs (UsbManager discovery and temporary permission, UsbDeviceConnection open/claimInterface/control/bulk transfers, getFileDescriptor intended for passing to native code) are public and documented.
what_it_establishes: The public authority path for an ordinary APK: user-approved access, exclusive per-interface claims, EP0 control and bulk transfers, and the documented native-code FD handoff. USB host support itself is feature-dependent per Google.
what_it_does_not_establish: That the target device exposes any particular device or interface, that claims or transfers succeed under its policy, or a universal public bus-reset API (none exists; UsbRequest excludes EP0 and has no Java isochronous API). Device exposure and permission outcomes remain untested until USB-01.

claim: Native USB passthrough to the Terminal VM is announced as future work in Google's Terminal preview.
what_it_establishes: Google has not shipped hypervisor-level USB passthrough as of 2026-10-16; this justifies owning Android-side hardware access and the USB/IP-first architecture rather than waiting for passthrough.
what_it_does_not_establish: Any current passthrough capability. It must never be marked available or assumed as a dependency; if Google ships it, this claim and ADR-0001 reopen.

claim: The built-in Debian VM's actually booted kernel provides a functional USB/IP VHCI importer (with USB core, needed class drivers and non-root raw-USB access) on the target device.
platform_scope: Target Googlebook device; built-in Debian VM kernel
what_it_establishes: Nothing yet. Linux documents the importer contract (vhci-hcd depends on USBIP_CORE && USB) and WSL documents an explicit kernel prerequisite, but no retrieved evidence covers Google's VM kernel or module policy.
what_it_does_not_establish: That desktop Debian results, WSL, Termux, Haven's alternate QEMU VM or VirtualHere claims transfer to Google's VM; a positive result elsewhere is a control only. Missing tools are not proof of absence; absent support blocks the default profile rather than deferring silently.

claim: libusb_wrap_sys_device (since libusb 1.0.23) wraps an externally opened descriptor as a borrowed handle: the system descriptor must remain open until libusb_close, libusb_close does not close it, the wrapped device must not be reopened with libusb_open, and LIBUSB_OPTION_NO_DEVICE_DISCOVERY (1.0.27+) disables scanning and hotplug.
what_it_establishes: The documented ownership model for the exporter's authorized-FD path: the Java UsbDeviceConnection is retained strongly through native drain and libusb_close; wrapping grants no root, no arbitrary usbfs ioctls, and no cross-kernel transferable handle.
what_it_does_not_establish: Which usbfs operations Googlebook permits on a granted descriptor, reset permission, speed reporting, kernel-driver detach, cancellation under detach, or NDK ABI/page-size compatibility on the target; an API declaration proves none of those.

claim: The ESP32-S3's native USB Serial/JTAG is fixed-function hardware documented to support bidirectional serial console, flashing, and JTAG debugging performed simultaneously with serial operations; USB-OTG and USB-Serial-JTAG share one internal PHY usable by only one controller at a time, a distinct constraint.
platform_scope: ESP32-S3 hardware (Espressif documentation; ESP-IDF v6.1 stable pages retrieved 2026-10-16)
what_it_establishes: Simultaneous CDC+JTAG on the native controller is documented capability (distinct from the shared-PHY OTG exclusion); documented behaviors include deep-sleep disconnect, light-sleep unresponsiveness, console buffering and boot-mode recovery. The S3 does not support SWD.
what_it_does_not_establish: That this operates through the GBCode USB/IP route on Googlebook, achievable JTAG speed, or board connector/pinout specifics. Concurrency remains a mandatory physical gate; a board's separate CP210x/CH34x UART connector is not evidence of native JTAG.

claim: A separately selected external programmer/debug adapter with its own supported target is a mandatory profile in addition to the ESP32-S3's built-in controller.
platform_scope: External JTAG/serial adapter hardware (Espressif JTAG guidance)
what_it_establishes: Espressif requires an external adapter compatible with target voltage and OpenOCD for external debugging; the S3's built-in JTAG controls only that chip, and S3 lacks SWD, so an external SWD probe satisfies the external profile with its own supported target, never the S3.
what_it_does_not_establish: Which adapter/target the project certifies (U02.01 selection with recorded voltage, pinout, backend and licenses), or that a probe family name guarantees compatibility.

claim: The inspected userspace USB/IP exporter candidates contain concrete source-level production gaps: usbipdcpp acknowledges reset commands without performing a physical reset and maps distinct libusb errors to EPIPE; the Rust candidate discards failed transfer results and lacks in-flight cancellation in its command loop.
platform_scope: Upstream candidate repositories at pinned commits (usbipdcpp fcb76a45, jiegec/usbip 61938f8c), inspected 2026-10-16
what_it_establishes: Actionable source findings that must be fixed or honestly gated before production selection; neither candidate is production-approved. usbipdcpp's authorized-FD example and async libusb paths are a reasonable first experimental base; the Rust CDC fixture supports synthetic importer investigation.
what_it_does_not_establish: Hardware failure or target infeasibility (the gaps are code findings), a complete security audit, NDK build evidence, or that any exporter works against Google's VM; candidate-source review may proceed without hardware.

claim: Code-OSS source is MIT-licensed, but Microsoft's product distribution, branding (name/icon) and Visual Studio Marketplace access are separate rights not granted by the source license; Marketplace access is not permitted to alternative products built on forks.
platform_scope: Upstream licensing and branding (Microsoft and Code-OSS documentation)
what_it_establishes: The legal boundary for GBCode: independent name and icon, a permitted registry (e.g. Open VSX) and authorized VSIX acquisition; source reuse does not confer Microsoft product identity, and manual VSIX installation does not override extension licenses.
what_it_does_not_establish: Rights to any particular proprietary extension or Microsoft service (Remote-WSL/SSH, Live Share, Settings Sync, proprietary debuggers/AI); each artifact needs its own license and compatibility check.

claim: In VS Code's web + remote topology, the browser runs a web-worker extension host and the remote server runs a Node extension host; the web client has no local Node extension host, and main/browser entry points plus extensionKind govern placement.
what_it_establishes: Browser extensions lack Node APIs and child processes (workspace.fs only; fetch subject to CORS); Node extensions execute in the Debian-side remote host; client and server versions must match exactly; UI-only Node extensions record honest unsupported results rather than manifest overrides.
what_it_does_not_establish: That every user extension works in this topology, or that remote placement gives extensions access to the Android native bridge (extension frames must never receive it).

claim: Exact upstream source identities for backend candidates are recoverable without cloning: code-server v4.141.0 (published 2026-10-08) embeds Code 1.141.0 via gitlink 2a59476c9bfcb90b3ddc372c36762471b7dfad1c; OpenVSCode Server v1.109.5 (published 2026-02-20) targets upstream 1.109.5 (072586267e68ece9a47aa43f8c108e0dcbf44622); code-server's About-dialog commit is its own repository commit, not the embedded upstream revision.
platform_scope: Backend candidate release metadata (GitHub APIs and pinned files, retrieved 2026-10-16)
what_it_establishes: Resolvable clean upstream controls per candidate, enabling the paired exact-source comparison procedure; the observed release-age gap (OpenVSCode older) is a recorded freshness concern, not proof of abandonment.
what_it_does_not_establish: Binary reproducibility, target execution, dependency provenance or security-patch coverage, and no production winner is selected; GitHub marked both latest releases immutable:false, so resolved commits and artifact hashes, not tag names, must be recorded.

claim: Physical host identity: HP Googlebook 14 running Android 17 (SDK 37), build HP/quartz/quartz:17/CL3B.260622.276.R2/16560795:user/release-keys, security patch 2026-09-01.
what_it_establishes: First physical evidence recorded in this ledger, distinct from all DOC entries: observed via ADB development tooling on 2026-10-16 (development probe only, not an application runtime dependency). Fixes the environment-identity baseline required by S00/S00.02 for all later probes.
what_it_does_not_establish: Guest Debian identity, ABI or kernel (still uninventoried), build-host capabilities, or persistence of these values across OTA updates; re-record after any system update.

claim: Host CPU ABI observed as arm64-v8a on the physical device.
what_it_establishes: APK native libraries for this device must target arm64-v8a; this is the Android ABI, distinct from the guest Linux architecture, which must be inventoried separately from inside the VM (uname-based, still unknown).
what_it_does_not_establish: x86_64 translation availability, the guest architecture, or build-host architecture; an APK ABI is never inferred from a Chrome user agent or Debian uname.

claim: Host userspace page size observed as 4096 bytes.
what_it_establishes: This unit currently runs 4 KB pages. 16 KB-alignment policy work (P16/R62: Play updates targeting >= 35 on 64-bit devices need 16 KB support by 2027-02-01) remains a separate packaging decision tracked against that deadline.
what_it_does_not_establish: Guest page size, future host policy, or exemption from 16 KB compatibility requirements for Play-distributed builds; runtime 16 KB compatibility still requires the documented ELF/APK checks.

claim: Installed WebView provider: com.google.android.webview version 149.0.7827.5 (package targetSdk 36).
what_it_establishes: The renderer identity that all WEB-probe fixtures must record alongside their evidence; every WebView result is valid only against this provider/version pair.
what_it_does_not_establish: Renderer feature behavior (secure context, workers, service workers, WebSocket, clipboard, IME) or local-network permission behavior toward the renderer; the target-36 vs 37 enforcement matrix remains an open NET-03 gate.

claim: Terminal app installed as com.android.virtualization.terminal v17 (targetSdk 37, minSdk 37) running as uid u10_a204; at observation time a crosvm_ToscanaMicrodroid VM process and virtualizationservice were running.
what_it_establishes: The shipping package identity and a live VM stack observed on 2026-10-16: Terminal present at v17 with minSdk 37, an associated crosvm VM process, and virtualizationservice running. Confirms the platform lineage inspected in SOURCE entries GB-PLAT-003/005.
what_it_does_not_establish: Lifecycle semantics (survival across tab close, task removal, force-stop, lock, sleep, reboot is LIFE-scenario scope), guest identity, or any control interface; a running VM at observation time is not evidence of window-independent lifetime (GB-PLAT-006 stays ROADMAP).

claim: Antigravity package com.google.android.apps.antigravity is installed on the device.
what_it_establishes: Physical confirmation on this unit of the pre-installation that P03/R03 document for supported models; the dual-grant user workflow (GB-PLAT-010) is demonstrable here.
what_it_does_not_establish: Any Antigravity API, service contract or entitlement to its AI features (Google account/AI plan and regional eligibility are Antigravity's own requirements, not GBCode's), and no behavior of Antigravity was exercised.

claim: Developer options and USB debugging (ADB) were enabled on the device during observation.
what_it_establishes: The ADB channel used for these observations is legitimate on this unit for development diagnostics, consistent with R63's development-tool scope.
what_it_does_not_establish: Any production dependency on ADB: ADR-0001 bans ADB from the product's normal runtime path, and end-user devices cannot be assumed to have debugging enabled.
